meta.description: Not Julia Child. Harriet Van Horne, a TV critic, opened a 1956 Vogue recipe piece with it. Traced to Vogue, 15 October 1956, p. 122.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Cooking is like love. It should be entered into with abandon or not at all'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Julia Child — Harriet Van Horne wrote it to open a Vogue article in October 1956. The misattribution came decades later.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1920–1998 · American newspaper columnist and television critic
answer.sourceLine: Van Horne opened a Vogue article titled ‘Not for Jiffy Cooks’ with this sentence on 15 October 1956. Quote Investigator traced it to that issue and verified the citation on microfilm ↗, and found no earlier appearance. It is not Julia Child’s line, though that is where the internet usually files it.

source.heading: A television critic’s recipe column

docMeta.dd: ‘Not for Jiffy Cooks’, by Harriet Van Horne
Vogue, 15 October 1956, p. 122, col. 1 (Condé Nast, New York)
‘Six recipes, simple, honest, and sometimes unconventional’
Verified — Van Horne’s own opening line

source.excerpt:
Cooking is like love. It should be entered into with abandon or not at all.

This, then, is not a document for jiffy cooks. Nor for those devotees of those premixed, prewhipped, pre-stewed foods that crowd the grocer's shelf.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ gives the earliest evidence as ‘1956 October 15, Vogue, Not for Jiffy Cooks by Harriet Van Horne, Start Page 122, Quote Page 122, Column 1, Conde Nast Publications, New York’, marked ‘Verified on microfilm’. The 1956 microfilm is not reachable from this session, so the primary citation here rests on QI’s verification, not on our own reading of the page.

QI’s conclusion is unambiguous: ‘evidence indicates that Harriet Van Horne created this saying and published it by 1956’, and ‘the words were assigned to Julia Child at a much later date perhaps because she was a prominent chef.’
Van Horne was a newspaper columnist and radio and television critic ↗ at the New York World-Telegram and later the New York Post — not a food writer, which is part of why the line drifted to a chef.
source.cutTag: Opening of ‘Not for Jiffy Cooks’, Vogue, 15 October 1956
source.excerptNote: Van Horne wrote it with a full stop — ‘Cooking is like love. It should be…’ The version in wide circulation substitutes an em dash (‘Cooking is like love — it should be…’), which is how the 2002 and 2007 printings below both render it.

author.name: Harriet Van Horne
author.heading: About Harriet Van Horne
author.metaLine: 1920–1998 · American newspaper columnist, radio & television critic
author.bio: Harriet Van Horne (1920–1998) was born in Syracuse, New York, graduated from the University of Rochester in 1940, and spent her career reviewing radio and television — first for the New York World-Telegram, later as a syndicated columnist in the New York Post. She was a Peabody Awards juror, covered the 1960 Nixon–Kennedy debates, and earned a place on Nixon’s list of political opponents. One colleague described her as ‘a dainty, blue-eyed blonde with a sweet-voiced feminine manner — and a harpoon in her typewriter.’

misattribution.heading: Who it gets handed to instead
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most reliably mis-credited lines in food writing. Quote Investigator documents two wrong names ↗, one printing that gives up and calls it anonymous, and one knowing adaptation.

items.why: The usual modern credit, and the reason most people meet the line at all. QI concludes the words ‘were assigned to Julia Child at a much later date perhaps because she was a prominent chef’ — it records a 2011 reader finding web pages crediting both Child and Van Horne, with no source offered for Child.

Nick Stellino’s Glorious Italian Cooking (Penguin, 2002), p. 39, printed the line in its em-dash form over the name SYDNEY SMITH — the English cleric and wit who died in 1845, more than a century before Van Horne wrote it.

A 2007 Post and Courier review of a new edition of The Silver Palate Cookbook noted the book carried the line ‘credited simply as graffiti on a kitchen wall’ — an honest shrug rather than a false credit, but it is how the attribution got lost.

items.scope: A deliberate variant, not a misquote
items.why: Los Angeles Magazine reported in February 1998 that the proprietors of a Californian lodge had reworked the adage for their dining room as ‘DINING OUT IS LIKE LOVE; IT SHOULD BE ENTERED INTO WITH ABANDON OR NOT AT ALL’ — knowingly adapted, and credited to nobody.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Harriet Van Horne’s, written to open a Vogue recipe article on 15 October 1956, and no earlier use has been found ↗.

context.heading: Written against convenience food
lead: The sentence is not a greeting-card sentiment — it is the opening salvo of an argument. Van Horne follows it immediately with ‘This, then, is not a document for jiffy cooks’, and then with a swipe at ‘premixed, prewhipped, pre-stewed foods that crowd the grocer’s shelf’. In 1956, at the high tide of American convenience food, ‘abandon’ was a position: cook properly or order in, but do not half-do it from a box.
context.detailsSummary: Why a TV critic was writing recipes
detailsBody: Van Horne’s day job was television. She reviewed it for the New York World-Telegram and the New York Post, sat on the Peabody Awards jury from 1958 to 1967, covered the 1960 Nixon–Kennedy debates as a TV critic, and was well enough disliked by Nixon to make his master list of political opponents. The best-known thing she ever wrote is a sentence about cooking, published under a subtitle promising ‘six recipes, simple, honest, and sometimes unconventional’.
context.pull: This, then, is not a document for jiffy cooks.

sourcesVerified.claim: Earliest evidence is Vogue, 15 October 1956, 'Not for Jiffy Cooks' by Harriet Van Horne, start page 122, quote page 122, column 1, Conde Nast, marked 'Verified on microfilm'; the article opens with the sentence and continues 'This, then, is not a document for jiffy cooks.'

QI concludes Van Horne created the saying and that it was assigned to Julia Child at a much later date; it also documents the 2002 Sydney Smith credit (Nick Stellino's Glorious Italian Cooking, p. 39), the 2007 'graffiti on a kitchen wall' label, and the 1998 Margaret and Tom Grade 'dining out' variant.

Harriet Van Horne (May 17, 1920 - January 15, 1998) was an American newspaper columnist and radio and television critic who wrote for the New York World-Telegram and the New York Post, served on the Peabody Awards jury 1958-1967, covered the 1960 Nixon-Kennedy debates, and appeared on Nixon’s opponents list.

Julia Child's debut cookbook Mastering the Art of French Cooking was published in 1961 by Alfred A. Knopf and her television programme The French Chef premiered in 1963 - so she had published no cookbook when the line appeared in Vogue in October 1956.
